the world's most endangered seahorse

By: Jason Boswell | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
a look at conserving the world's most endangered seahorse...

Unique Selling Point:
The Knysna Seahorse is only found in three estuary systems in South Africa, and is currently the only seahorse in the world listed as endangered by the IUCN. A team of researchers are hoping their research will allow the animal to be better protected...

Summary:
The Knysna Seahorse is the only seahorse in the world currently listed as endangered by the IUCN and its tiny habitat is continually being threatened by human development. Despite this being an iconic species in South Africa there is still a lot we don't know about it - however, one scientist is leading a research project in Knysna to learn more about the species and to help save it from possible extinction.

According to the lead researcher:

"It should be remembered that the Knysna Estuary is the most important estuary in South Africa in terms of biodiversity – and if active management of our estuary and its catchments are not done – we might be losing a national asset."

She runs a research group called the Knysna Basin Project which is starting a pilot project commencing in late May where her and her team will be tagging seahorses underwater with tiny UV tags in order to understand the animals' home range which she hopes will lead to the creation of new seahorse reserves. She hopes that the Knysna Project can be used as a pilot project which other South African coastal towns can follow to help preserve their environments.

The main threats to the seahorse are habitat loss due to human development but also other factors that go along with it - including how human activity affects the water quality - its the management of the areas that's crucial to the long term survival of the seahorse. But another point which the researchers are looking at is whether the seahorses are adapting...or indeed thriving...in the artificial waterways of Thesen Island, Knysna's biggest development.

Additional voices I think could include a representative from local government about how the seahorse is consideration for further development in Knysna and the surrounding estuaries, a representative from industry who's developing the area and perhaps a town representative about the iconic importance of the seahorse to the town.

Further information:
In terms of filming we'll be able to film the researchers working on various studies involving the seahorse including:

One student physically scooping up samples of a naturally occurring seagrass to check how many seahorses are using this traditional habitat versus the artificial matts at the bottom of the Thesen Island waterways.

The lead researcher searching for and tagging seahorses underwater using tiny UV reflective tags to track the seahorses' range.

We could also speak to the Cape Town aquarium as they have the only artificial breeding population of the seahorses which are also exported to zoos worldwide to further research on the animal.

Extra Budget Items:
Travel and accommodation for team in Knysna.

Press Release:


Knysna Seahorses
The Knysna Seahorse is officially the world’s most endangered seahorse and also South Africa’s only endemic species. But how are researchers trying to save this iconic
animal? Carte Blanche explores the underwater habitat of these reclusive creatures

Script:


Script Visuals
VO: Bridging the gap between mountain and ocean, the Knysna Lagoon is one of South Africa’s most iconic waterways.

This unique ecosystem supports a myriad of life…both above….and below the water…

And the estuary is also home to a rather reclusive, but famous, animal…
Wides of Knynsa Lagoon, bird life, some underwater footage of eelgrass beds…

Day 4



LINK 0772: The Garden Route has become world-reknowned for whale-watching and diving with Great White Sharks…but now there’s a much smaller creature that’s attracting attention….The Knysna Seahorse….


VO: Louw Claassens heads up the Knysna Basin Project and is one of the continent’s leading seahorse researchers….
Set up shots of Louw on the Beach




UPSOUND Louw Claassens CLIP 0806

It’s South Africa’s only endemic seahorse species…now across the world there’s probably around 40 or 41species, so this is OUR species…(Derek interjection) so we can be proud? I think so…I would be…I am…um…and it’s the first seahorse, and still the only one, listed as endangered on the IUCN Red Data List of threatened species, so it’s very important internationally to protect this species.

They are very charasmatic and we are just getting started to know what goes on with our Knysna seahorse.
Shots of RECCE Dive looking for seahorses combined with murky macro shots.



Seahorses are actually a fish and are unqiue in the way in which the male is the one who gives birth. The female transfers eggs to him which he then fertilises and stores for between two to four weeks before givng birth…and then the young are pretty much on their own.
Derek Question: Clip0807: So what has lead to the seahorse becoming endangered?


UPSOUND: Louw Claassens

See it only occurs off three estuaries off our coast, the Knysna Lagoon, Keurbooms and the Swartvlei – so it’s that limited range, small population size, and then habitat vulnerability – these guys do depend on eel grass vegetation and the live in shallow estuarine habitats and that’s the places we like to live, we like to play and we change the habitat from natural to artifical so they lose a lot of habitat.
Underwater seagrass…Louw snorkelling…
VO: all three of the estuaries where the seahorse lives falls within the Garden Route National Park…and its up to Paddy Gordon and his team to manage manging these sensitive waterways…
UPSOUND Paddy

We remained concerned…We encourage a lot of research, to make sure we make the right decisions…we work with stakeholder bodies to make sure we monitor the quality of the water, the amount of pollution and of course SAN Parks manages the entire waterbody of the Knysna Estuary, and as such we can control fishing, bait collecting, boating activities and even developments along the lagoon…
Footage of Lagoon – signage about water quality, boats
VO: Thesen Island is one of Knysna’s most prestigious areas with luxury homes lining the development’s waterways… and initially its construction was controversial from an environmental perspective… Wides of Thesen Island
LINK: CLIP0813 But now there’s a twist in the tale of the Knysna Seahorse it seems there are some elements of this island’s construction that work in its favour…
V/O : Reno Mattresses and gabions are rock-filled wire structures that were used in the construction of the island’s waterways…Now they appear to be a sanctuary for the seahorses… Underwater Gabion footage…
Louw Claassens: In this specific case yes the the materials the developers used…the reno mattreses and gabion walls do provide a novel new habitate and going forward we’ll see if the population is better off in this artificial habitat than in the natural eel grass habitat…



V/O The latest research seems to show a higher density of seahorses in these man-made structures…


Seahorse release…
LINK: Seahorses are known for their fluctuations in populations, and you need long-term monitoring to know if they’re thriving or merely surviving…the question is..how do you track a seahorse?


Trying to find these little seahorses in murkey water is quite challenging…but a new tagging project could be the answer…

LOUW: The idea is to use a liquid elastomer, and we use a curing agent to let it harden and the cool part is it fluoreces and that helps with underwater…

DEREK…And you can have different colours…

and what makes seahorses so perfect for this type of tagging is that they have various location on their bodies….

DEREK: How can you be sure you’re not harming the seahorses in any way?

It is an invasive tagging method, but the concept is that it’s injected under these bony plates so it’s just under the skin and the good thing is that once you inject it once it stays there and it’s a long term tagging method…



Craig Smith says Thesen Island’s human population has become quite protective of their little new neighbours…


UPSOUND Craig Smith, Environmental Chair, Thesen Island Marina Homeowner’s Association..

It’s always easy when you talk about a whale or something bigger…but I think the seahorse is one of the best guides for us to show us how good our water quality is…

One of the conservation measures we’ve put in place – sort’ve no wake zones so you don’t get the wash onto the gabions which could harm the seahorses…

It’s been a case of education, most of the residents here bought it as a holiday home and didn’t really have much interest in the ecology, but with the education and with the talks that we give…





No wake zones…Thesen Island…

VO: While most are fairly optimisic on the seahorse’s future, there have been some other suggestions on how to preserve this particular species….






LINK: 0771: The Knysna Seahorse breeds quite well in capitvity, but there are challenges when you try introduce these fellas into the wild…the big waterways…
VO: Over 1000km away scientists at uShaka Sea World have had a population of Knysna Seahorses in their exhibit for nearly 30 years…Dr Judy Mann-Lang says while breeding programmes can be a viable option for other endangered species the seahorse’s situation is a little more complicated…



UPSOUND CLIP Dr. Judy Mann-Lang

“People often say well why don’t you just breed a lot of them and then everything will be fine…well it’s not that easy, there’s two things to think about…”

“The first thing is you need to look at what happens if you introduce an animal into the wild, is it disease free? So we need to look at the disease risks, are the genetics of the captive and wild population the same so are we not maybe changing the genetics of the wild population.

We need to check on that – so that’s what we need to check on before we even consider introducing a species back into the wild.

Then the other thing is that you don’t want to put all that effort into breeding these animals, release them into the wild and find that the environment is so degraded that they die anyway.

So habitat restoration, looking after the habitat is really first prize before any type of reintroduction could even be considered.
VO: While a breeding programme isn’t being implemented at the moment, for the time being the people of Knysna feel protecting the existing wild population is far more important…
Question: Reverses: At current rates do you think the Knysna Seahorse could die out?
LOUW: I would think so yes…I mean it’s a small population, it’s fragmented they’re not densely populated or evenly distributed…and if their habitate is not protected, if this species isn’t protected then yes it could die out…how quickly is another matter…and then if it’s not immediate then people tend to forget about it…but yes, conservation needs to be implemented…

The other matter is…we know what the denisyt is…we don’t know the total popualtion size is…and that’s what people like to know ‘how many seahorses are there’ well we don’t know…Derek: and whthere they’re thriving or merely surviving

…if they’re actually functioning! So our aim going forward now is…to establish what the population number…what their size is…and comparing that between habitat types, artificial versus natural…and how far they move…and once we establish that we can actually work towards reserves and protecting specific areas…




Promos
15 Seconds
1.) VO: The Knysna Seahorse is one of the country’s most reclusive animals and has been called the most endangered seahorse in the world…
UPSOUND – Louw Claassens “It was the first, and still the only seahorse on the IUCN’s Red Data List of Endangered Species…
2.) Over the past few years researchers, authorities and the local residents have been working to try save Knysna’s iconic species…
VO: (10 seconds)
10 seconder
What works for some endangered species, doesn’t apply to the Knysna Seahorse…

UPSOUND Judy Mann-Lang: “People often say well why don’t you just breed a lot of them and then everything will be fine…well it’s not that easy…”

The lead researcher searching for and tagging seahorses underwater using tiny UV reflective tags to track the seahorses' range. We could also speak to the Cape Town aquarium as they have the only artificial breeding population of the seahorses which are also exported to zoos worldwide to further research on the animal.
